channel.description: Silverado Trail → Petrified Forest → Calistoga Rd → Santa Rosa → Sebastopol → Bohemian Hwy. Play episodes in order as you drive.

item.title: 01. Welcome aboard: leaving the capital
item.description:
Good morning, Julia! Good morning, Adam! And a big hello to our trusty driver. I'm your guide for today, a proud NorCal local, and I am stoked to show you around. We're going from the capital to the redwoods: across a floodplain, over the hills into wine country, and down to the Russian River at Guerneville. I'll pipe up when there's something good, and I'll keep quiet when there isn't.
Okay, first quiz of the day, nice and easy. Before the levees went up, Sacramento flooded so often that the city did something kind of wild about it. What do you think they did? … They raised the streets. A wh

item.title: 02. Sam Brannan, California's first millionaire
item.description:
Okay, here's a name you're going to hear all day: Sam Brannan. Total character. He was a printer and a Mormon elder who sailed a whole shipload of Latter-day Saint emigrants around Cape Horn to California in 1846, and he packed a printing press and an entire flour mill for the trip. He started the California Star, San Francisco's first newspaper, and he's considered the first guy to spread the word about the Gold Rush. Then his stores supplied the rush, and boom: California's first millionaire.
He bought land everywhere, including a hot-springs valley at the top of Napa Valley that he named C

item.title: 03. West Sacramento: the Town of Washington
item.description:
Alright, first town of the day, and what a way to start. Picture it: 1849. A guy named James McDowell starts a bar fight, and loses it fatally. He leaves behind his wife Margaret, three daughters and 600 acres. And Margaret? She doesn't fall apart. She hires a surveyor, carves the land into forty-one blocks, and sells lots in a brand-new town she names the Town of Washington. Total boss move.
That's where you are now: West Sacramento, in Yolo County. Washington became a rest stop for exhausted travellers slogging through the marshes to Sacramento, and a busy fishing town, shipping salmon, stu

item.title: 04. The Yolo Bypass: a floodplain on purpose
item.description:
Okay, look out the windows, both sides. All that flat land? This is one of the cleverest bits of flood control in America, and you're driving right over it on the Yolo Causeway, a three-mile-long bridge.
Here's the trick. Instead of building taller and taller walls around Sacramento, engineers just gave the river somewhere else to go. Upstream there's a concrete spillway called the Fremont Weir. When the Sacramento River gets too high, the extra water simply pours over the top, into this basin. In a big flood this whole area becomes a shallow inland sea, about forty miles long and three miles

item.title: 05. The causeway, the Tule Jake Road, and a quarter of a million bats
item.description:
Want to know who lives under this bridge? Have a guess. … Bats! Roughly a quarter of a million Mexican free-tailed bats migrate to the Yolo Causeway every June. They squeeze into the expansion joints between the concrete sections and feast on bugs from the wetlands. It's one of the biggest bat colonies in California, and there are actual bat-watching tours at dusk.
Before any causeway existed, crossing this basin in the wet season meant a ferry, or a long detour south through Stockton. In summer, the first vehicle to make it across set the route of the Tule Jake Road. The first causeway opene

item.title: 06. Davis: the university farm
item.description:
Coming up is Davis, and here's a quiz for you, Adam and Julia. Davis is famous for one particular way of getting around. Any guesses? … Bikes! It's so flat that it calls itself the bicycling capital of America, and it's even home to the United States Bicycling Hall of Fame.
Davis started out as a railroad stop in 1868, named Davisville after a local farmer, Jerome C. Davis. Then in 1907 the post office got tired of all those extra syllables and just chopped it down to Davis. Classic.
The big deal here is the university. Back in 1905 the state picked Davis from about fifty sites for a univers

item.title: 07. UC Davis and the wine revolution
item.description:
Okay, wine nerds, this one's for you. UC Davis keeps popping up in the wine story all day. Back in 1903 the federal government set up an experimental vineyard at Oakville, in the Napa Valley, and UC Davis still runs it. In 1935, the Wolfskill family, the farming pioneers of Winters, gave the university a hundred acres of their old ranch for an experimental orchard.
Quiz: in 1951, UC Davis produced its very first graduates in the science of growing grapes and making wine. How many were there? … Just seven! And one of them, Joe Heitz, went on to make one of Napa's most famous Cabernets, Martha'

item.title: 08. The Gold Rush, and how it remade this whole region
item.description:
Okay, let's talk about the event that made Sacramento, and, honestly, most of what you'll see today.
On the 24th of January 1848, James Marshall was building a sawmill for the pioneer John Sutter, up the American River, when he spotted something shiny in the water. Gold! Sutter tried to keep it secret, because he was worried a rush would wreck his plans for a farming empire. Quiz: who do you think spread the news anyway? Hint: you've already met him today. … Sam Brannan! And about 300,000 people poured into California. San Francisco went from about 200 people in 1846 to around 36,000 by 1852,

item.title: 09. Tule fog: the valley's winter ghost
item.description:
Here's a handy one if you ever drive this valley in winter. From November to March, after the first big rains, the Central Valley gets something called tule fog, named after the tule reeds that used to cover the wetlands.
On long, still winter nights, the damp ground cools fast, and the cold air near the ground gets trapped under warmer air above, until it turns into a thick, low blanket of fog. It can stretch over 400 miles, from Bakersfield to Red Bluff. Quiz: in 2005, tule fog was the number one cause of what in California? … Weather-related car accidents! So if you ever see this valley di

item.title: 10. Dixon: the town that moved to the tracks
item.description:
Here's a fun one. Dixon, coming up, is a town that literally picked itself up and moved.
During the Gold Rush there was a little settlement called Silveyville around here, a halfway stop for miners heading between the coast and the gold fields. Then the railroad showed up in 1868, and it missed Silveyville by a few miles. Awkward. So in 1871 the whole town just relocated, buildings and all, to sit next to the tracks. The Methodist church on North Jefferson Street made the trip.
Quiz time. The new town was supposed to be called Dicksville, after Thomas Dickson, who donated the land for the de

item.title: 11. Why the valley is so flat: seven miles of buried sea floor
item.description:
Okay, geology time, and I promise this one's cool. Question: why is this valley so ridiculously flat? … Because you're driving across the top of a giant filled-in hole.
Back when dinosaurs were around, between about 150 and 65 million years ago, this whole valley was a seaway. To the east, where the Sierra Nevada is now, there was a chain of volcanoes. To the west, an ocean plate was diving under North America, and the rocks scraped off it piled up into a ridge that worked like a dam. In between was a deep basin, and the volcanoes eroded straight into it, sending mud and sand down underwater

item.title: 12. The Patwin: the people of this valley
item.description:
Let's rewind way, way back. Long before the farms, the freeway and the bikes, this edge of the Sacramento Valley belonged to the Patwin, the southern branch of the Wintun peoples, who've lived around here since roughly the year 500.
They lived in settled villages, fishing, hunting and gathering, and the big one was acorns. All those oak groves on the plains and foothills? That was the harvest. Here's something cool: their group names are still all over today's map. The Ululatos lived where Vacaville is now, around a village on Ulatis Creek. The Labaytos lived along Putah Creek, the Malacas in

item.title: 13. The railroad that beat the Golden Spike
item.description:
Okay, here's a story with a twist. Quiz first: when the transcontinental railroad was finished with the famous golden spike in May 1869, where did it actually end? … Sacramento! Not the Pacific. Getting trains the rest of the way to San Francisco Bay was a whole separate race.
And the tracks beside this freeway? They won a part of that race. They were built by the California Pacific Railroad, to link Vallejo, on the bay, with Sacramento. The line was finished in November 1868, six months before the golden spike, so from early 1869 you could take a ferry from San Francisco to Vallejo and catch

item.title: 14. Interstate 505: the highway that lost its letter
item.description:
Fun fact: the road you've just turned onto used to have a letter in its number! This is Interstate 505, a quiet four-lane road running about thirty miles up the edge of the valley to Interstate 5. Basically, it lets people skip Sacramento entirely.
It was originally planned as part of a loop called I-5W, W for west. Then the feds scrapped almost all the lettered interstates and chopped I-5W into pieces. One piece became the stretch of I-80 you just drove, and this piece became 505. The northern end only opened in 1977.
That ridge to your left is the Vaca Mountains. The flat ground you're on

item.title: 15. The Nut Tree: a fruit stand that fed a Queen
item.description:
Coming up near the junction with Interstate 505 is the Nut Tree. Today it's a shopping centre, but it used to be a legit California legend.
It opened on the 3rd of July 1921 as a tiny fruit stand on the old Lincoln Highway, run by Helen and Ed Power. It's named after a black walnut tree that grew from a nut a pioneer girl, Sallie Fox, picked up on a trail in Arizona before she got here in 1859.
The stand blew up. By year two it was serving around 950 cars a day. Then it grew into a restaurant with a floor-to-ceiling glass aviary, a bakery, a toy shop, and its own little train out to its own

item.title: 16. The Delta: California's Holland
item.description:
South of the freeway, out of sight, is one of the most important places in California: the Sacramento-San Joaquin River Delta. The Yolo Bypass floods drain into it, and so does about half of all the water that runs off California's land.
Here's how it formed. Around 560,000 years ago, water broke through the coastal mountains and carved the Carquinez Strait and San Francisco Bay. All the rivers had to squeeze out through that one narrow gap, which slowed them down. The tides pushed back up and slowed them even more, so the rivers dropped their mud and built a huge freshwater marsh full of cha

item.title: 17. Vacaville and the quarrel over Rancho Los Putos
item.description:
Coming up is Vacaville, and its founding story is a little shady. Here's how it went down.
In 1841, two guys from New Mexico, Juan Manuel Vaca and Juan Felipe Peña, came to California, and in 1843 they were granted a huge ranch called Rancho Los Putos: over 44,000 acres, stretching almost all the way to Davis. Peña's adobe house, built in 1842, is still standing, the oldest building around here.
Then in 1850, Vaca sold some land to a man named William McDaniel, on the condition that a square mile would become a town called Vacaville. McDaniel's business partner, a lawyer, acted as interprete

item.title: 18. The Vaca Mountains: the first wall of the Coast Ranges
item.description:
See that ridge rising up to the west? Those are the Vaca Mountains, the very first wall of California's Coast Ranges, and the thing standing between this flat valley and all the wine country we're about to see.
Quiz: once we cross over those hills, everything gets a lot greener. Why do you think that is? … Rain shadow! The Vacas are the furthest range from the ocean, so the clouds have already dropped most of their rain on the mountains further west. That's why the ridgetops here are dry chaparral: chamise, manzanita and buckbrush.
The east face of the Vacas shoots straight up, a thousand fe

item.title: 19. From the Lincoln Highway to Interstate 80
item.description:
This road you're on has had a few identities. In 1913, the Lincoln Highway was dedicated: the dream of an Indiana entrepreneur, Carl Fisher, and one of the first highways in America built for cars, running all the way from Times Square in New York to San Francisco. In 1928, it was rerouted across the Yolo Causeway and through Davis, Dixon, Vacaville and Fairfield, pretty much where you are right now.
Then it became Highway 40, and roadside spots like the Nut Tree fruit stand grew up along it. In the fifties and sixties it was rebuilt as Interstate 80, the main coast-to-coast route from New Yo

item.title: 20. Jelly Belly: the President's jelly beans
item.description:
Okay, this is one of my favourites. Fairfield is the home of the Jelly Belly! And the story goes from Germany all the way to the White House.
Gustav Goelitz started a candy business back in 1869, and the family got big making candy corn. His son Herman moved west and ended up in Oakland in 1924. In the 1960s they started making tiny, super-flavourful mini jelly beans. And guess which famous fan got hooked on them? … Ronald Reagan! He'd quit smoking and taken to sweets instead. As governor in 1973, he wrote to the company that they could hardly start a meeting without passing the jar around.

item.title: 21. Fairfield, Cordelia, and a captain's sense of home
item.description:
Fun fact about the next two towns: they were both named by the same guy, a clipper ship captain called Robert H. Waterman. He named Fairfield after his hometown back in Connecticut. And in 1853 he started a little settlement he called Bridgeport. When the post office asked for something more original, he renamed it after the most important person in his life. Any guesses? … His wife, Cordelia! Aww.
Waterman also pulled off a sneaky political move. In 1858 he entered Fairfield in the race to become the county seat, and won it away from Benicia, helped by offering sixteen acres of free land for

item.title: 22. The Rockville Stone Chapel and a congregation split by war
item.description:
Just north of Cordelia, in the Suisun Valley, there's a little stone church with a big story: the Rockville Stone Chapel, built by volunteers in 1856. The stone is volcanic ash rock from the nearby hills, and it's soft and easy to cut when it comes out of the ground, then hardens once it's exposed to air. How handy is that?
The land was donated by Landy Alford, who came west in 1846 in the same wagon train as the famous Donner Party, and his son-in-law later helped rescue the survivors.
Then the Civil War split the church. The congregation divided over slavery, and on Christmas Eve 1863, the

item.title: 23. The Suisun Marsh
item.description:
Off to the south is a place where people tried to farm for about fifty years, and gave up because it got too salty even for the cows. That's the Suisun Marsh, described as the biggest brackish-water marsh on the whole west coast: over a hundred thousand acres of tidal marsh and sloughs, where fresh river water meets the salty bay. It's named after the Suisunes, a Patwin group who lived here.
During the Gold Rush, hunters shot ducks and geese here to sell fresh birds and feathers in San Francisco's markets. From the 1880s, farmers built levees and tried to grow crops, until the soil got too sa

item.title: 24. Jameson Canyon: through the hills on the Lincoln Highway
item.description:
Okay, fun thought for this stretch: you're driving through old sea floor. This is Highway 12 through Jameson Canyon, the gap in the hills between Solano County and Napa, and back in 1928 it became part of the Lincoln Highway, the first road across America.
Check out the rocks. The geological maps show Markley Sandstone along here, white to light-grey, around 40 to 50 million years old. Further west come marine sandstones from the late Miocene, including one called the Cierbo Sandstone, which has beds of fossil shells in places. So these hills are basically old beaches and sea floor, folded up

item.title: 25. Entering the Napa Valley
item.description:
Welcome to the Napa Valley, everybody! This is the big one. In 1981 it became only the second official wine region in the whole country, and now it's one of the most famous wine regions on the planet, with more than 450 wineries.
Quick lay of the land. The valley floor rises gently from sea level here near the bay up to Calistoga at the far end, at the foot of Mount Saint Helena. Mountains on both sides: the Mayacamas on your left as we head north, and the Vacas on your right. And two roads run up the valley: Highway 29 on the west, and the quieter Silverado Trail on the east.
Quiz! Where do

item.title: 26. di Rosa: moonshine, mushrooms and modern art
item.description:
Hidden off this road is the di Rosa art centre, and the land has had quite a life.
In 1855 someone planted grapes and olives here. In 1886 two Frenchmen built a stone winery. Then the phylloxera bug killed the vines, and the old winery got used for growing mushrooms, making moonshine, storing grain, and finally as a hay barn.
In 1960, Rene di Rosa bought it, replanted vines and turned an old Depression-era pond into a 35-acre lake. When he sold the vineyards in 1986, he used the money to turn the whole place into an art park. Now it has about 1,600 works by Northern California artists, in ga

item.title: 27. General Vallejo: the man in the middle
item.description:
Okay, one man pops up in almost every story on this side of the hills: Mariano Guadalupe Vallejo. Let's meet him properly.
He was born in Monterey in 1807, the eighth of thirteen kids of a Spanish soldier. As a boy he got private lessons from the governor, with access to his library, and an English merchant taught him English, French and Latin. In his twenties he was sent north to close the Sonoma mission and command the whole northern frontier. He became super powerful and super rich, with a ranch of 44,000 acres.
He was a man stuck between two worlds. In 1846, the Bear Flaggers took him pr

item.title: 28. Napa: a river town
item.description:
Picture Napa's Main Street in the 1850s: up to a hundred saddle horses tied up on any old afternoon. Yeehaw.
The city of Napa, off to the east, started life as a river town. The Napa River is tidal here, so this was as far as boats could get. The first recorded ship came up in 1842, and by 1850 a steamer called the Dolphin was carrying passengers. Nathan Coombs laid out the town in 1847 and 1848, and in 1859 John Patchett opened the county's first commercial winery, selling wine for two dollars a gallon. Two bucks!
There's a darker side to the story, though. When the first recorded expeditio

item.title: 29. Floods, gentrification and the goddess of plenty
item.description:
For most of its history, Napa was the town wine tourists drove straight through. That changed after a 300-million-dollar flood project around the turn of this century widened the river and raised the bridges, and the developers moved in.
The big showpiece was Copia, a center for wine, food and the arts, mostly paid for by Robert and Margrit Mondavi and named after the Roman goddess of plenty. It opened in November 2001, with galleries, theatres, a giant kitchen garden and a restaurant called Julia's Kitchen, backed by Julia Child herself. But the crowds never came, and it closed in 2008. Juli

item.title: 30. The Silverado Trail: cinnabar, Black Bart and a marathon
item.description:
You're on the Silverado Trail, the quieter road up the east side of the Napa Valley, 29 miles long. And quiz: back in the 1880s, travellers on this road had to watch out for a famous someone. Who? … A stagecoach robber called Black Bart! He preyed on travellers here. Things got safer when a motor bus service started in 1910.
The road started in 1852 as a trail used when floods made the main valley road impassable. Later it became the wagon road for the mercury mines on Mount Saint Helena, and the first permanent road between Napa and Calistoga. Silver was found in the valley in 1858. Today th

item.title: 31. The Wine Train and Brannan's railroad
item.description:
Keep an eye out for the Napa Valley Wine Train, which runs from Napa to St. Helena right alongside Highway 29. And believe it or not, this train went all the way to the California Supreme Court.
The tracks are old. Sam Brannan, our Gold Rush millionaire, started the Napa Valley Railroad in 1864 to haul tourists from the Vallejo ferries up to his hot-springs resort in Calistoga. Passenger service ended in 1929. Then in the 1980s, when Southern Pacific wanted to abandon the line, local entrepreneurs bought it for 2.5 million dollars to run a fancy tourist train with lunch and wine.
A lot of lo

item.title: 32. Stags Leap: the Cabernet that beat Bordeaux
item.description:
Okay, wine fans, sit up! You're about to pass the vineyard that beat the French. This is the Stags Leap District, a tiny pocket of land only about one mile by three, with hills on three sides.
Here's the story. Warren Winiarski fell in love with wine while spending a year in Italy studying Machiavelli. He moved his family to Napa in 1968 and worked at Robert Mondavi's new winery. Then he tasted a homemade wine from a neighbour, Nathan Fay, and thought, this is it. In 1970 he bought the 44 acres next door. Quiz: what was growing on the land when he bought it? … Prunes, cherries and walnuts! He

item.title: 33. Yountville: the trapper who planted the first vines
item.description:
Coming up is Yountville, named after George Calvert Yount, and this guy's life was basically a Western movie.
Born in North Carolina in 1794, he fought in the War of 1812, then left his family in Missouri to become a fur trapper. He reached California in 1831, hunted sea otters off the Channel Islands, then worked as a carpenter for General Vallejo in Sonoma. Through Vallejo he got a huge land grant in 1836 and became the first permanent Euro-American settler in the Napa Valley. And in 1838, he planted the valley's very first grapevines. So, Yount: the guy who started all of this.
Here's a s

item.title: 34. The French Laundry and the bubbles from Champagne
item.description:
Okay, foodies, this one's for you. Yountville is home to The French Laundry, one of the most famous restaurants in America. And yes, it really was a laundry. The stone building went up as a saloon in 1896. Then in 1906 a law banned alcohol near the Veterans Home, and in 1920 it became a French steam laundry.
In 1978 Sally Schmitt and her husband Don, who was the mayor at the time, turned it into a restaurant and kept the old name because locals still called it that. Sally was a pioneer of California cuisine, cooking with local, seasonal ingredients. Thomas Keller took over in 1994 and won thr

item.title: 35. Who does the work? Farm labour in the valleys
item.description:
Every vineyard and orchard you pass depends on people who rarely show up in the wine brochures. Here's their story.
The first workers were Native Californians, often forced. The Patwin were made to work for free on ranches and in mines, and by 1870 only a few Native people remained in the Napa Valley, working as labourers and servants. In the late 1800s, Chinese and Japanese immigrants worked Vacaville's orchards. In World War Two there was even a camp of German prisoners of war near Windsor, put to work.
The biggest change was the Bracero Program, a deal between the U.S. and Mexico that sta

item.title: 36. How the Napa Valley was built: volcanoes, faults and gravel
item.description:
Let's talk dirt! Because in this valley, the dirt is literally the product.
Shape first. Napa is a long, skinny trough between two mountain ranges, with a whole family of faults, including the West Napa Fault, slicing through and slowly sliding the land past itself.
Then: volcanoes! Between about eleven and three million years ago, this whole area was erupting. The leftovers are called the Sonoma Volcanics, lava, ash and broken volcanic rock, and the hills on both sides are full of it. There's even a low hill east of Napa that geologists think was a volcano rising up inside an old collapsed

item.title: 37. The Franciscan Complex: California's geological junk drawer
item.description:
Okay, here's California's geological junk drawer: the Franciscan Complex, and much of the Coast Ranges from here to the ocean is made of it.
For tens of millions of years, an ocean plate was diving under North America, and as it went down, it scraped off a crazy mix of stuff: deep-sea sandstone, chert full of tiny fossils, ocean-floor basalt, and chunks of rock that got dragged deep underground, squeezed under enormous pressure, then popped back up. Geologists call it an accretionary wedge, and the Franciscan is the textbook example.
Quiz: there's a rock in here called mélange. That's French

item.title: 38. Why the Napa Valley isn't covered in houses
item.description:
Have you noticed something about the Napa Valley floor? There are basically no housing developments or shopping malls between the towns. That's not luck. It's one of the most important land decisions in California history.
Neighbouring counties let big stretches of farmland turn into houses and shops. But in 1968, Napa's winemakers and civic leaders went the other way. Using a new state law that gave tax breaks for keeping land in farming, they created an agricultural preserve on the valley floor. Quiz: was Napa the first county in California to do this? … Yes! It was the first one in the sta

item.title: 39. Lake Hennessey and the valleys behind the hills
item.description:
This little lake lent its name to the fire at the heart of California's seventh-largest wildfire complex. Here's the story.
This is Lake Hennessey, the City of Napa's main water supply. Congress approved a dam here in 1944 but never paid for it, so in 1946 the city just built it themselves, for 550,000 dollars. It's named after Edwin Hennessey, a local leader who helped get it done.
Early on the morning of the 17th of August 2020, a lightning strike started a small fire on Hennessey Ridge Road near the lake. The Hennessey Fire grew to 192,000 acres all by itself, the heart of the LNU Lightni

item.title: 40. Frog's Leap and Joe Heitz: jokes, organics and the turning point
item.description:
Two wineries along here tell two sides of the Napa story.
First, Frog's Leap, started in 1981 by a doctor and a winemaker at a spot known as Frog Farm. Quiz: the winemaker got his start at a very famous winery nearby. Can you guess which, from the name? … Stag's Leap! Frog Farm plus Stag's Leap equals Frog's Leap. And the corks say Ribbit. But behind the jokes, it's serious stuff: it was the first Napa winery to use certified organic grapes, the vines aren't irrigated, and since 2005 solar panels supply most of its power.
Then Heitz Cellar, from 1961, back when Napa had only about two dozen

item.title: 41. Bust: phylloxera, Prohibition and the Depression
item.description:
Okay, the Napa crash story. By 1880, this valley was booming: hundreds of vineyards, and by 1900 more than 140 wineries. Then came three punches in a row.
Punch one was tiny. A bug called phylloxera, a louse that eats grapevine roots, killed vines all over the valley. The fix was planting vines on roots that the bug couldn't hurt.
Punch two: Prohibition, in 1920. Lots of wineries just closed. A few survived making wine for churches, and growers sold grapes to people making wine at home.
Punch three: the Great Depression.
The comeback was slow, helped by a French winemaker at Beaulieu, Beri

item.title: 42. The Wappo: the brave ones
item.description:
Long before vineyards, this valley was Wappo country. Their homelands covered the Napa Valley, the south shore of Clear Lake, the Alexander Valley and the Russian River valley.
They lived in small, independent groups, hunting and gathering, in homes made of branches, leaves and mud. And their baskets were woven so tightly they could hold water. Acorns from the oaks were a staple, and the hot springs up at Calistoga were a place of healing.
I love the old Wappo place names. Quiz: the Wappo called the area around St. Helena Anakotanoma. What do you think it means? … Bull Snake Village! Calisto

item.title: 43. St. Helena: Beringer, Krug and the castle of wine
item.description:
Welcome to St. Helena, the heart of old Napa wine country, and quiz time! One of the valley's first great vineyards here came out of a very modern-sounding legal document. What do you reckon? … A prenup! Charles Krug started his winery here in 1861, often called the valley's first. He married Dr. Bale's daughter, and her mum insisted on a prenuptial agreement that protected twenty acres north of town. And that's exactly where Krug planted his vines. Smart lady. Much later, the Mondavi family bought the Krug winery for 75,000 dollars.
Then there's Beringer, founded in 1876. It calls itself the

item.title: 44. The happy accident of White Zinfandel
item.description:
Here's one of the great accidents in wine history. Right on Highway 29 in St. Helena is Sutter Home. In 1948 the Trinchero brothers bought it and scraped by making cheap jug wine.
In 1972, Bob Trinchero started making a pale wine from red Zinfandel grapes. Then, in 1975, about a thousand gallons of the juice stopped fermenting before all the sugar was gone. Oops! He set it aside, tasted it two weeks later, and it was sweet, pink and, in his words, pretty good. Quiz: what famous wine had he just accidentally invented? … White Zinfandel! By 1987 it was the best-selling premium wine in America.

item.title: 45. The Judgment of Paris
item.description:
Okay, this is the big one. The story that put Napa on the world map.
In the early seventies, some California wines were amazing, but nobody cared, because everybody wanted French labels. A British wine merchant in Paris, Steven Spurrier, set up a blind tasting for America's 200th birthday. On the 24th of May 1976, eleven judges, mostly French wine experts, tasted the best Chardonnays and Cabernets, French versus Californian, without knowing which was which. Spurrier assumed France would win.
Quiz! What happened? … California won both! Top white: a 1973 Chardonnay from Chateau Montelena, just

item.title: 46. Howell Mountain: gold medals from the hilltops
item.description:
Look east around St. Helena. That forested ridge is Howell Mountain. And here's a surprise: Napa was winning medals in Paris long before 1976!
Two French winemakers set up there in 1877, and Charles Krug planted about a hundred acres by 1884. Then a man called W. S. Keyes planted his vineyard in 1880. Quiz: at the Paris Exposition of 1899, what did his wines win? … Gold and bronze medals! And in 1904, his claret won the grand prize at the St. Louis World's Fair. So 1976 wasn't the first time Napa impressed the French. It was just the most famous.

item.title: 47. Spring Mountain: a mountain that isn't one
item.description:
You're climbing Spring Mountain Road into the Mayacamas. Quiz: where's the actual Spring Mountain? … Trick question! There isn't one. Spring Mountain was the name for a whole green, well-watered area of hills full of springs and little streams, not one peak.
It was one of the first places in Napa recognised for grapes. The first documented vineyard was Charles Lemme's La Perla, planted in 1874, and in the 1880s the Beringer brothers planted up here too. The vineyards are on steep slopes, so the crops are small: it makes less than two percent of Napa's wine. Up over the county line, the road b

item.title: 48. The Bale Grist Mill and the redwoods of Bothe
item.description:
Here's a cool spot coming up: the Bale Grist Mill, with its giant 36-foot waterwheel. It's one of only two water-powered mills left west of the Mississippi. And there's evidence that the rebels of the 1846 Bear Flag Revolt met here before they marched on Sonoma!
It was built in 1846 by Dr. Edward Turner Bale, an English ship's doctor who became surgeon-in-chief of the Mexican army and married General Vallejo's niece. His land stretched all the way from Rutherford to Calistoga. Settlers came from across the valley to grind their corn and wheat here, and the old-timers swore the slow-ground mea

item.title: 49. Castles, cable cars and caves
item.description:
Okay, the road into Calistoga has some seriously over-the-top wineries.
First: Castello di Amorosa, an actual medieval-style castle, opened in 2007. It has 107 rooms, a moat, a drawbridge, a great hall with frescoes, and wait for it, a torture chamber with an iron maiden that the owner says he bought in Italy for 13,000 dollars. In the 2020 fire, the farmhouse burned, but the castle was fine. Of course it was. It's a castle.
Next: Sterling Vineyards, perched on a volcanic hill 300 feet up. Quiz! How do you get up to the winery? … An aerial tramway! Like a ski lift. And the building looks lik

item.title: 50. Who gets to say Calistoga? The politics of wine labels
item.description:
Two wineries went to war with the federal government over one word: Calistoga!
Here's the deal. Official wine regions are created by the federal government, and once one exists, wineries have to use mostly grapes from that area to put its name on the label. In 2003, Bo Barrett of Chateau Montelena asked for a Calistoga wine region. But two wineries, Calistoga Cellars and Calistoga Estate, already had Calistoga in their brand names. Quiz: what do you think they'd have to do if the region was approved? … Either use at least 85 percent Calistoga grapes, or change their names! They fought it hard

item.title: 51. Calistoga: a slip of the tongue
item.description:
Welcome to Calistoga, at the top of the Napa Valley! Julia, Adam, this town has my favourite origin story of the day. Quiz: how do you think it got its weird name? Have a think. … It was a slip of the tongue! Sam Brannan, our Gold Rush millionaire, visited the hot springs here in 1852, fell in love, and bought more than 2,000 acres to build a spa to rival the fancy Saratoga Springs in New York. The story goes he meant to call it the Saratoga of California, but it came out as the Calistoga of Sarafornia. True or not, the name stuck!
His resort opened in 1862, and his railroad arrived in 1868,

item.title: 52. Robert Louis Stevenson's squatter honeymoon
item.description:
Here's a romantic one. In 1880, a broke, sickly Scottish writer showed up here with his new American wife. Quiz: who was he? He wrote Treasure Island. … Robert Louis Stevenson! He'd crossed an ocean and a continent to marry Fanny Vandegrift Osbourne, and friends told him the mountain air up here would help his lungs.
They tried the fancy Hot Springs Hotel, but couldn't afford ten dollars a week. So they spent their two-month honeymoon squatting, with Fanny's twelve-year-old son, in an abandoned bunkhouse at an old silver mine called Silverado, up on Mount Saint Helena. Cloth over the windows,

item.title: 53. Mount Saint Helena and the Russian princess
item.description:
Look north, everyone. That big mountain closing off the top of the valley? That's Mount Saint Helena. It has five peaks in a rough letter M, the Napa River starts on its slopes, and it's one of the few mountains around the Bay Area that actually gets snow.
Okay, quiz, and this one's a curveball. The Wappo called it Human Mountain, and the Spanish called it Mount Mayacamas. But the name it has today came from a completely unexpected country. Which one? … Russia! In 1841 a Russian survey party from Fort Ross, out on the Sonoma coast, climbed to the top and left a copper plate with the name of P

item.title: 54. Hot ground: the Sonoma Volcanics, Clear Lake and The Geysers
item.description:
Here's a fun fact to blow your minds: you're crossing the Mayacamas Mountains, and almost everything around you was once molten.
The rock is called the Sonoma Volcanics: obsidian, pumice, ash, and lava, several thousand feet thick. It makes up most of the mountains around the Napa and Sonoma valleys, and it erupted from several vents, on and off, mostly between three and five million years ago. It's also what a lot of the wine-country soil is made of. So: lava wine. Kind of.
And the volcano story isn't over! To the north, around Clear Lake, is a volcanic field that last erupted only about 11

item.title: 55. The Petrified Forest: redwoods turned to stone
item.description:
Coming up on, wait for it, Petrified Forest Road, is the Petrified Forest. About 3.4 million years ago, an eruption from the direction of Mount Saint Helena buried a forest of giant redwoods in volcanic ash. And over thousands of years, those trees turned to stone. Stone trees!
Quiz! The biggest one, nicknamed The Queen, is eight feet wide and 65 feet long. How old do you think she was when the volcano got her? … About 2,000 years old! And here's the twist: these redwoods prove that redwoods used to grow way further inland than they do now.
Fun history too. Robert Louis Stevenson visited on

item.title: 56. Wine country on fire: 2017, 2020, and the insurance crisis
item.description:
Driving through these hills, you might spot blackened tree trunks, and brand-new houses where old ones used to be. Here's the story of the fires.
On the night of the 8th of October 2017, hot, dry winds were gusting up to seventy miles an hour, and more than a dozen wildfires broke out across Northern California. One of them started at 9:43 at night near Tubbs Lane, just north of Calistoga. The Tubbs Fire raced more than twelve miles in its first three hours, through the Mark West Springs area and right into Santa Rosa. It destroyed more than 5,600 buildings, half of them homes in Santa Rosa.

item.title: 57. The Rodgers Creek Fault: the Hayward Fault's northern half
item.description:
Okay, a little earthquake talk. Somewhere under this part of Santa Rosa runs one of the most dangerous faults in the Bay Area.
You've probably heard of the Hayward Fault, under Berkeley and Oakland. Well, this side of the bay has its partner: the Rodgers Creek Fault, running right through Santa Rosa. In 2016 scientists showed the two are actually connected under San Pablo Bay, making one fault about 120 miles long, from north of Healdsburg all the way to San Jose. It's the kind of fault where the ground on the other side slides sideways, to your right.
Quiz: on the evening of the 1st of Octo

item.title: 58. The Grape King of California
item.description:
Here's a wine story you won't hear in many tasting rooms.
California's first wine grape was the Mission grape, brought by the Spanish, and it ruled until about 1880. Then the Gold Rush created thirsty customers, and Agoston Haraszthy brought in cuttings from 165 of Europe's best vineyards. Charles Krug, a Prussian political dissident, learned winemaking from Haraszthy before starting his own winery in St. Helena.
And north of Santa Rosa, at the utopian colony of Fountain Grove, the vineyards were run by Nagasawa Kanaye. Quiz: what nickname do you think he earned? … The Grape King of Californ

item.title: 59. Santa Rosa: the slaughtering place and the Carrillo adobe
item.description:
Welcome to Santa Rosa, the biggest city in California's wine country! And it has a creek with a pretty grim name. Let me explain.
Before Europeans arrived, the Santa Rosa plain belonged to a powerful Pomo group called the Bitakomtara. They controlled it tightly: outsiders needed permission to pass through, and if they didn't ask, the penalties were harsh. They gathered for ceremonies on Santa Rosa Creek, near today's Spring Lake. Colonisation brought violence, enslavement and smallpox, and devastated them, though their descendants still live in the region.
The first European home here was bu

item.title: 60. Charles Schulz, Snoopy and the ice rink
item.description:
Okay, Peanuts fans! Santa Rosa was home to Charles Schulz, the creator of Charlie Brown and Snoopy. He grew up in Minnesota, the son of a barber, loved ice hockey, and moved out here in 1958. He kept drawing Peanuts right up until he died in 2000.
In 1969 he and his wife built an ice rink here, and everyone calls it Snoopy's Home Ice. Quiz: what do you think the café inside the rink is called? … The Warm Puppy! Every summer it hosts Snoopy's Senior World Hockey Tournament for older players from around the world.
Down the street is the Charles M. Schulz Museum, with a 22-foot mural made of 3,

item.title: 61. Luther Burbank: the plant wizard of Santa Rosa
item.description:
Near downtown Santa Rosa is the house and garden of Luther Burbank, one of the most famous plant breeders who ever lived. And Julia, Adam, there's a really good chance you've eaten his work.
He was born in Massachusetts in 1849, the thirteenth of fifteen kids. As a young man he bred a new potato, sold the rights for 150 dollars, and used the money to move to Santa Rosa in 1875. Inspired by Charles Darwin, he crossed plants on an enormous scale and created more than 800 varieties: the Shasta daisy, the Santa Rosa plum, a white blackberry, a spineless cactus for cattle.
Quiz: a natural variant

item.title: 62. Believe It or Not: Robert Ripley of Santa Rosa
item.description:
Believe it or not, Robert Ripley was born right here in Santa Rosa, in 1890. He left high school after his dad died, started drawing sports cartoons for newspapers at sixteen, and moved to New York in 1913. In 1918 he drew his very first Believe It or Not cartoon, all about weird facts and feats, and readers loved it. They started mailing him their own oddities: funny-shaped vegetables, strangely marked pets, you name it.
He took his facts seriously enough to hire a full-time researcher. And by 1929 the panel was running in 360 newspapers in 17 languages, followed by radio and TV shows. Quiz:

item.title: 63. The Pomo: the people of the Russian River
item.description:
This river is Pomo country. The Pomo lands once stretched from the Pacific coast all the way inland to Clear Lake. But here's the thing: the Pomo were never one single nation. They lived in small, independent bands linked by family, and they spoke seven related languages so different that speakers of one couldn't understand another.
Quiz: the name Pomo was originally the name of just one village. What do you think it meant? … Those who live at red earth hole! Probably after the red magnesite they mined to make beads, or the reddish soil. By 1877, English speakers were using it for everyone.

item.title: 64. The Coast Miwok
item.description:
The land from the Golden Gate up to the Sonoma coast, and east to Sonoma Creek, was home to the Coast Miwok. That includes the hills around Sebastopol and Freestone and the lower Sonoma Valley.
They lived in small bands with no central government. In spring they headed to the coast for salmon, shellfish and seaweed. The rest of the year, acorns were the staple, plus deer and rabbit. Quiz: Coast Miwok hunters had a clever trick for sneaking up on deer. What do you think they did? … They rubbed themselves with a plant called Brewer's angelica to hide their scent! They also drank yerba buena tea

item.title: 65. Sebastopol: a bar fight and the Gravenstein apple
item.description:
Welcome to Sebastopol, which has one of the best name stories on the map. Quiz: the town was originally called Pine Grove. Then in the late 1850s, a bar fight broke out. And somehow that led to the new name. How? … A bystander said the long, drawn-out brawl was like the siege of Sevastopol, a Russian port in the Crimean War. And the name stuck! Remember Yountville? It was going to be called Sebastopol too, but this town got there first.
The Coast Miwok and Pomo were here first, and the town sits on top of several of their village sites. Later there was a busy Chinatown downtown from the 1880s

item.title: 66. Burbank's Gold Ridge farm and the electric railway
item.description:
Luther Burbank, our potato guy, needed more space than his Santa Rosa garden, so in 1885 he bought a farm here in the Gold Ridge area. Quiz: at its peak, how many plant experiments do you think he had going on this farm at once? … Over 60,000, by some estimates! Three acres of it survive, with more than 250 of his plants, looked after entirely by volunteers.
And Sebastopol used to have electric trolleys! From 1903 to 1947, the Petaluma and Santa Rosa Railway ran around the county, partly to break the big railroad's monopoly. All that's left is one passenger car in a museum, and its old stone

item.title: 67. The Russians in California
item.description:
We've met Russians again and again today: a river, a mountain, a farm near Graton. So here's the whole story.
Russian traders pushed east across Siberia and the North Pacific, and in 1799 they set up a colony in Alaska. Their business was fur, especially sea otters. From 1803, American ship captains took Alaska Native hunters down the California coast to hunt otters, and between 1805 and 1812 alone they gathered over 22,000 pelts.
In 1812 the Russians built their own base, Fort Ross, on the Sonoma coast, in the land of the Kashaya Pomo. It was super diverse: Native Californians, Native Alask

item.title: 68. Cannabis: California's other crop
item.description:
Wine isn't the only crop around here with a complicated legal history.
California has been at the front of cannabis politics for half a century. In 1972, it held the first ballot vote in the nation to legalise cannabis. Quiz: did it pass? … Nope! It failed. But in 1996, California became the first state to legalise medical cannabis, and in 2016, voters legalised recreational use, with 57 percent of the vote.
Legalisation turned out to be messy. Growers had to register and get permits, and more than half of the medical dispensaries closed. Legal businesses pay hefty taxes, while illegal growe

item.title: 69. Freestone: the innkeeper who burned the bridge
item.description:
Freestone, population about thirty-two, is the gateway to the Bohemian Highway. It's named after a sandstone quarry, and it was the first historic district Sonoma County ever named, in 1974.
And it has my favourite crime story of the trip. In 1876, a farmer built the Hinds Hotel here when he heard the railroad was coming, and the carpenters building the railway line stayed there. Quiz: according to first-hand reports, the innkeeper came up with a sneaky plan to keep his guests around longer. What did he do? … He had parts of the bridge they were building secretly burned at night, so the job w

item.title: 70. Occidental: Dutch Bill, sawmills and a commune deeded to God
item.description:
This next town has a creek named after a sailor who jumped ship, and a commune that tried to give its land to God. Welcome to Occidental!
It was founded in 1876 as a stop on a railroad from the Sausalito ferry up to the redwoods. A local landowner, a Danish sailor known as Dutch Bill Howard, who'd jumped ship in San Francisco Bay in 1849, gave the railroad its right-of-way. In return he got a free lifetime train pass, and the station was named after him. The creek next to the road is still Dutch Bill Creek. The railroad started a timber boom, and by 1877 there were six sawmills here.
Then, a

item.title: 71. Camp Meeker: the logger's subdivision
item.description:
Quiz: how much would you pay for a plot of land twenty-five feet by twelve, with a one-room cabin on it? … In 1898, right here, it cost seventy-five dollars. This is Camp Meeker, named after Melvin Cyrus Meeker, a lumber baron who opened mills here around 1866. These redwoods built San Francisco, and then, after 1906, rebuilt it. Meeker is the same guy who sold the Bohemian Grove land to the Bohemian Club. Once the trees were cut down, he chopped the land into those tiny lots and sold them to San Franciscans wanting a summer escape.
Now it's a little village of about 425 people tucked among t

item.title: 72. Bohemian Grove: the most exclusive campsite in America
item.description:
Okay, conspiracy fans, this one's for you. Just downstream at Monte Rio, hidden in the redwoods, is the Bohemian Grove: a 2,700-acre private campground owned by San Francisco's very exclusive Bohemian Club. Every July, powerful people from politics, business and the arts spend more than two weeks camping here.
It started innocently. In 1878, a bunch of journalists from the club had an overnight going-away party in the redwoods for an actor moving to New York. They had so much fun they did it again the next year, without him! Then the rich businessmen joined, and the money and the power follow

item.title: 73. Day two: river, ocean, redwoods, bridge
item.description:
Good morning, road-trippers! Day two. Mike's on driving duty, Adam and Julia are in charge of snacks, and I'm in charge of the chat.
Here's the plan. We follow the Russian River to the ocean, then drive down the wild Sonoma Coast to Bodega Bay, where Hitchcock made birds terrifying. Then either along Tomales Bay and Point Reyes, or inland through Petaluma, to the giant redwoods of Muir Woods. And finally over the Golden Gate Bridge, through San Francisco, to the airport.
Big trees first, if you've got an hour before you leave: Armstrong Redwoods is just north of Guerneville. The Parson Jones

item.title: 74. Korbel: Bohemian brothers and California champagne
item.description:
Okay, wine lovers, up ahead is a winery that legally prints the word champagne on its labels, and France can't do anything about it.
It's Korbel, making sparkling wine here since 1882. It was started by Francis Korbel and his brothers, who came from Bohemia, and who also, randomly, started a satirical San Francisco magazine called The Wasp. They use the proper Champagne method, where the wine gets its second fermentation right in the bottle you buy.
So how do they get away with saying champagne? … Old American rules from the 1930s treat some place names as semi-generic, as long as the label

item.title: 75. Rio Nido: there is no Canyon Five
item.description:
Here's one of my favourite little places: Rio Nido, the river nest, a tiny resort village tucked into a redwood canyon. It was started in 1908 by a San Francisco lodge called the Eagles, so its first name was Eaglenest. In World War Two, its dance hall was packed with sailors on leave and big bands played there.
Okay, Julia, Adam, here's a weird one. The streets here are named Canyon One, Canyon Two, Canyon Three, Canyon Four, then Canyon Six and Canyon Seven. What's missing? … There's no Canyon Five! The story goes it's because of an accident on the road that became Canyon Six. Spooky.
And

item.title: 76. Guerneville: from Stumptown to resort town
item.description:
Ladies and gentlemen, Julia, Adam and our amazing driver: welcome to Guerneville! You made it! Woohoo!
Okay, pronunciation check. It's Gurn-vill. Locals even sell T-shirts that say Don't call it Guerneyville. So now you know.
Final quiz of the trip. The town's very first English name was a bit less pretty. Given that loggers cut down most of the giant redwoods here in the late 1800s, what do you think they called it? … Stumptown! And the parade every year is still called Stumptown Days. The redwoods grew so thick here that local legend says the valley had the densest amount of living stuff o

item.title: 77. Armstrong Redwoods: the trees the loggers missed
item.description:
If you've got an hour, go see the trees that the loggers missed: Armstrong Redwoods, just north of town. In the 1870s, Colonel James Armstrong saved the grove as a natural park. After he died, his daughter and another local family ran a whole campaign, with rallies and car caravans, to save this last bit of the old forest, and in 1917 the county bought it for 80,000 dollars.
